caseno: Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No.108 of 1994
lawyer:
AW Bhuiyan, Addition Attorney-General instructed by B Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------  For the Petitioner.
Kh. Mahbub Hossain, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court, instructed by Mvi. Md. Wahidullah, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Respondent.
parties:
State ------ Petitioner 
vs
MA Malik ------ Accused-Respondent
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal J: This petition by the State is from judgment and order dated 28 August, 1994 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Criminal Misc. Case No.1402 of 1994 enlarging the accused-respondent on anticipatory bail to the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet and further directing him to surrender before the Court below within 14 days. 

 2. Respondent filed an application under section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure praying for anticipatory bail in connection with Sadar Kotwalli P.S. Case No. 4 dated 2.3.93 under section 6 of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance pending in the Court of Thana Magistrate, Sadar, Sylhet. 

 3. Facts of the case, briefly, are that the respondent was admittedly married to one Sultana Jasmin Khan (Shaopa) daughter of Abdul Mukit Khan of Sylhet town on 11.10.1991 the aforesaid lady filed a petition to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet on 28.2.1993 against the respondent and his relations alleging that it transpired shortly after their marriage that the respondent was a greedy man of loose moral character. At the instigation by other accused persons he put pressure upon her to bring dowry of Taka one crore from her father and started threatening her in various ways. Her father was an Ex-Chairman of Sylhet Zilla Parishad and now a sitting Member of the Parliament. On 17.3.1992 the respondent went to her paternal house at Sylhet where she was then residing. At about 10 O'clock in the night in course of exchange of words on the question of payment of dowry the respondent became infuriated and physically assaulted her and attempted to kill her by strangulation. She was somehow saved by others in an unconscious condition. The matter was, however, amicably settled. Again on the night following 18.6.1992 while at his own residence at Dhaka the respondent on getting a negative reply from her regarding payment of dowry dealt a severe blow on her left ear causing profuse bleeding. On getting information her father came, took her to Sylhet and arranged for her treatment. Again there was some settlement and she came to live with the respondent at Dhaka. It was decided that the dispute would be finally settled after the return of the respondent from London where he was to go in connection with some business. He returned from London on 31.8.92 and in the meantime she had left for her father's house at Sylhet for better treatment. The respondent, however, refused to come to a compromise before payment of the dowry. She received the respondent's lawyer's notice dated 21.11.1992 demanding a huge amount to which she sent a reply. 

 4. The Deputy Commissioner sent the petition to the police station for necessary action and Police on 2.3.1993 starred the aforesaid case against the respondent. The learned Judges were informed by the learned Deputy Attorney-General at the time of hearing that the Police had already submitted charge-sheet on 22.8.1994 against the respondent under section 6 of the aforesaid Ordinance. 

 6. The respondent in his application for bail denied the allegation made in the petition to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet terming them as absolutely false and fictitious. He stated that he was a respectable citizen and a business magnate of the country having a number of Industries and Commercial enterprises and paying income tax to the tune of Taka 23 lacs approximately per year. He alleged that shortly after the marriage he could learn that before the marriage the informant had extra-marital affairs with some other person and that all attempts to normalise the relationship failed. He filed both Criminal and Civil cases against her and also divorced her on 15.8.1993. 

 8. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits that the High Court Division committed an error of law in entering into the merits of the case and granting anticipatory bail upon a finding that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of the offence which is based on no evidence causing serious prejudice to the prosecution. 

 10. As for the first submission, it is clear that the finding in question was not made on merit; it could not be, because evidence is yet to be led. The learned Judges evidently made the finding with an eye on section 497(1) CrPC for the purpose of bail only. This finding also answers the second submission made on behalf of the State. The learned Judges after noticing the particular facts of the case observed: 

 11. We have considered the special facts of the case, particularly the fact that the spouses are at loggerheads, both of them having taken recourse to Court and that there is possibility of the respondent being harassed in the circumstances stated by him in his petition and therefore, it is difficult to hold that the High Court Division exercised its discretion unreasonably or unfairly. There is no compelling reason to interfere with the impugned order.
